[[Category:Vector space]]
A '''linear map''', also known as a '''linear transformation''', is a [[function]] that maps one [[vector space]] to another, preserving addition and scalar multiplication.

== Formal definition ==

{{#content:Q2997}}

== Kernel ==

The '''Kernel''' of linear map $T$

$$
\ker T=\{\vec{v}\in V:T(\vec{v})=\vec{0}\}.
$$

<blockquote>
Note this is different from the definition of the [[kernel pair of a function]].
</blockquote>

== Properties ==

=== $T(\vec 0)=\vec 0$ ===

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
\forall \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{F}: T(\vec 0)=T(\alpha \vec 0 +\beta \vec 0)= \alpha T(\vec 0) + \beta T(\vec 0)=(\alpha+\beta)T(\vec 0)
$$

Since $\alpha+\beta \in \mathbb{F}$ is arbitrary

$$
T(\vec 0)=\vec 0
$$

is the only solution.
{{End hidden}}

==== Application ====

If $f(\vec 0) \ne \vec 0$, $f$ '''cannot''' be a '''linear map'''.

=== Composition ===

If $T_1,T_2$ are '''linear maps''', then $T_1 \circ T_2$ is also one.

{{Hidden proof}}
Write

$$
\forall \vec u,\vec v\in V,\forall \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}
\begin{cases}
T_1(\alpha \vec u+\beta \vec v)=\alpha T_1(\vec u)+\beta T_1(\vec v) \\
T_2(\alpha \vec u+\beta \vec v)=\alpha T_2(\vec u)+\beta T_2(\vec v)
\end{cases}
$$

Then

$$
T_1\circ T_2 (\alpha \vec u + \beta \vec v) \\
= T_1 (\alpha T_2(\vec u) + \beta T_2(\vec v)) \\
= \alpha T_1 \circ T_2(\vec u) + \beta T_1 \circ T_2(\vec v)
$$

So $T_1 \circ T_2$ is a linear map.
{{End hidden}}

=== Inverse ===

If $T:X \to Y$ is a '''linear map''' from $X$ to $Y$, then $T^{-1}:Y \to X$ is a linear map from $Y$ to $X$.

{{Hidden proof}}
Since $T:X \to Y$ is a linear map,

$$
\forall x_1,x_2 \in X: \\
T(\alpha \vec x_1 + \beta \vec x_2)=\alpha T(\vec x_1)+\beta T(\vec x_2)\\
\Rightarrow T^{-1} (T(\alpha \vec x_1 + \beta \vec x_2))=T^{-1}(\alpha T(\vec x_1)+\beta T(\vec x_2))\\
\Rightarrow \alpha \vec x_1 + \beta \vec x_2 = T^{-1}(\alpha T(\vec x_1)+\beta T(\vec x_2))\\
\Rightarrow \alpha T^{-1}(T(\vec x_1)) + \beta T^{-1}(T(\vec x_2))= T^{-1}(\alpha T(\vec x_1)+\beta T(\vec x_2))\\
$$

Since
$$
\forall \vec y_1, \vec y_2 \in Y: \exists x_1,x_2 \in X,\, T(x_1)=y_1, T(x_2)=y_2
$$

Hence

$$
T^{-1}(\alpha \vec y_1 + \beta \vec y_2)= \alpha T^{-1}(y_1)+\beta T^{-1}(y_2),\, \forall y_1,y_2 \in Y
$$

So $T^{-1}:Y \to X$ is a linear map from $Y \to X$.
{{End hidden}}

== Examples ==

Common linear maps include:

* Scaling by a scalar: $\vec{x}\mapsto \lambda \vec{x}$;
* Matrix multiplication: $\vec{x}\mapsto \mathbf{A}\vec{x}$;
* Composition of linear maps;

On [[coordinate space]]s:

* Rotation about the origin (change of [[vector space basis|basis]]);
* Projection onto a subspace;

On suitable [[function space]]s:

* Integration: $p\mapsto \int p$;
* Differentiation: $p\mapsto \dot{p}$;
* Evaluation at a fixed point: $p\mapsto p(a)$;

== Counterexamples ==

Common non-linear maps include:

* The [[norm]] $\vec{x}\mapsto \|\vec{x}\|$ is not linear.
* $\vec{x}\mapsto \vec{x}^{n}$ is not linear.
* Translation: $\vec{x}\mapsto \vec{x}+\vec{a}$ is not linear unless $\vec{a}=\vec{0}$
** ($T(\vec{0})=\vec{a} \neq \vec{0}$ unless $\vec a = \vec 0$)
